first_impression.reaction: Our daughter sent this after I asked whether a wedding overseas would actually count back home. I read it all on the iPad. The first paragraph told me straight away there's no licence here, there's a notice, and the celebrant registers it. Good. It reads like it was checked against the government websites, and it says plainly it isn't legal advice, which I respect. It's a paperwork page, written to the couple, so most of it is for my daughter rather than me. What I really wanted was in the last third: will the marriage be recognised, and will she be able to change her name. Nothing about deposits, contracts or getting Mum there, but I didn't expect that on a page like this. A few paragraphs are very dense, and two terms lost me.

journey.quote: If you are searching for a marriage licence in Australia, there is none to apply for.
journey.reaction: Straight to the point. I'd assumed there was a licence like in the American films. Now I know.

journey.quote: This is general information as at November 2026, not legal advice.
journey.reaction: Honest. I'd rather be told that than be given confident advice from a wedding company that turns out to be wrong.

journey.quote: If the wedding is less than a month away, a prescribed authority may approve the marriage going ahead.
journey.reaction: Who or what is a prescribed authority? I'd have to ring someone to find out. Not a worry for us, but it's the sort of phrase that makes me feel I'm reading a government form.

journey.quote: The practical lesson: lodge the notice once your date and celebrant are settled, rather than in the final month.
journey.reaction: That's the line I'll pass on to my daughter. Plain, sensible, and it stops a last-minute panic.

journey.quote: "I call upon the persons here present to witness that I, A.B. (or C.D.), take thee, C.D. (or A.B.), to be my lawful wedded wife (or husband, or spouse)", or words to that effect.
journey.reaction: Rather lovely, actually, to see the old words written out. Useful to know they must be said even if the big celebration is somewhere else.

journey.section: The certificates signed on the day
journey.quote: It is the one couples frame, but the commemorative certificate from your wedding day is not the official, legal marriage certificate.
journey.reaction: I didn't know that. I'd have assumed the one they hand you is the real one. That's worth knowing before anyone goes to the bank or Medicare with the wrong piece of paper.

journey.quote: You apply for a copy of your official marriage certificate from the registry, and your celebrant can do this on your behalf, generally at a cost.
journey.reaction: At what cost? Even a rough idea would help. Small, but I like to know what we're paying for.

journey.quote: As at November 2026, an Australian-authorised celebrant cannot perform an overseas marriage, and an overseas marriage cannot be registered in Australia.
journey.reaction: This is exactly what Geoff will ask. It's clear, though 'cannot be registered' gave me a jolt until I read further down that it is still recognised.

journey.quote: You apply online, then appear together in person before an agent no sooner than 30 days before the ceremony, each with valid government-issued photo ID.
journey.reaction: Useful, but this whole Hawaii paragraph runs on with 30 days this and 30 days that. I had to read it twice on the iPad to keep the two straight.

journey.quote: DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities only accept one issued in their own country, so ask the embassy or consulate whether you need a CNI, where to get it and whether it needs an apostille.
journey.reaction: Three sets of initials and the word apostille, which nobody explains. I'd be lost here. And it leaves it to the couple to chase the embassy. Who actually helps them with this?

journey.quote: An overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid in the country where it took place and would have been valid here.
journey.reaction: That's the reassurance I came for. I'll forward this paragraph to Geoff.

journey.quote: Plan the name change separately. Some states and territories do not accept overseas marriage certificates for a name change, and in NSW you apply for an official change of name instead, which does not mean the marriage is unrecognised.
journey.reaction: Good that it warns us, but it only names NSW. We're in Victoria. Does this apply to us? It tells me to ask the registry, so at least I know who to ring.

journey.section: Marry at home and celebrate abroad
journey.quote: The paperwork stays with you, your celebrant and the registry, while a Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments anywhere in the world, as your single point of contact from start to finish.
journey.reaction: Now that's clear about who is responsible for what. Legal side with the celebrant, everything else with one person. 'Payments' is the word I wanted, though I'd like to know how the deposits are handled.

journey.section: Plan your wedding abroad with Wedded Concierge
journey.quote: Whichever country makes it legal, one Wedded Advisor works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, and the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: AUD, in writing, before anything starts. That's what I need to hear when it's our money. Still no name or phone number, and no word on deposits.

turn_offs_found.quote: You apply online, then appear together in person before an agent no sooner than 30 days before the ceremony, each with valid government-issued photo ID. The ceremony must take place within 30 days of picking up the licence, which is valid only within the State of Hawaii, and the person who marries you must hold a licence from the Department of Health. There are no state residence or US citizenship requirements, and our Hawaii wedding guide sets out the timeline.
turn_offs_found.why: A long unbroken paragraph with two different 30-day rules in it. On the iPad it's a wall of text and I mixed the two up on first read.

turn_offs_found.quote: DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities only accept one issued in their own country, so ask the embassy or consulate whether you need a CNI, where to get it and whether it needs an apostille.
turn_offs_found.why: Initials and jargon with no explanation. It makes me feel I ought to know these things already, and I don't.

would_share_with: My husband, the 'generally recognised in Australia' paragraph and the 'cannot be registered in Australia' line together, so he stops worrying the marriage won't count
My daughter, the 'lodge the notice once your date and celebrant are settled' line and the warning that the ceremonial certificate is not the official one
My daughter again, the 'Plan the name change separately' paragraph, so she rings the Victorian registry before they book anything

cta_reaction.quote: Tell us your date, your guest list and where you would like to marry, and begin with Wedded Concierge.
cta_reaction.why: It isn't pushy and the AUD and fee-in-writing line just above it is right. But this page is about paperwork, not planning, so I wouldn't enquire from it. I'd forward it to Geoff, talk it over, and only go ahead if the first step is a phone call with a real person who can tell me how the deposits are handled.
